title.value: Structured Flow-Based Gridding and Upscaling for Reservoir Simulation

name.value: Stanford University, Department of Petroleum Engineering

note.value: Fine grid geocellular reservoir characterizations often include detailed descriptions of permeability heterogeneity as well as a high degree of geological and geometric complexity. When we construct coarse models for reservoir simulation based on these detailed geological representations, the use of flexible curvilinear grids enables the more efficient representation of important features in the reservoir. Upscaling methods that are compatible with these grids must also be applied. In this thesis, we develop and apply gridding and upscaling techniques to provide accurate coarse models. Our methodology is in the context of structured grids. For 2-D systems, we studied several grid generation techniques. We first considered streamline-based gridding with Laplacian smoothing to capture high flow regions effectively and with improved grid quality over pure streamline grids. Two other structured gridding methods (the Jacobian-based elliptic method and optimization-based method) were implemented and investigated to achieve better local control of grids and to incorporate additional information (not necessarily flow-based) into the grid generation procedure. Techniques for computing effective (or upscaled) properties for these grids were also implemented. We first developed a new finite element-based upscaling method to resolve the coarse cell geometry accurately. We also developed two finite difference-based upscaling procedures (permeability upscaling and transmissibility upscaling). These techniques offer an approximate treatment of the coarse cell geometry but display better computational efficiency than the finite element method. Comparisons of flow results using these upscaling methods show that the finite element-based and the finite difference-based methods have similar performance in terms of accuracy. For the 3-D implementation, we therefore implemented the more efficient finite difference methods. The gridding techniques implemented in 3-D include the streamline-based method with Laplacian smoothing and the Jacobian-based elliptic method. We extended permeability upscaling and transmissibility upscaling to 3-D and compared their performance (within the context of multipoint and two-point flux approximations, respectively) for several example cases. We evaluated our gridding and upscaling techniques for a variety of heterogeneous permeability fields generated by two-point and multipoint geostatistics with different domain shapes (Cartesian or non-Cartesian). We considered flow scenarios with different boundary conditions (linear flow or well-driven flow) and different fluid properties (single-phase or two- phase). These flow tests demonstrate that for many cases, the coarse models constructed by the combination of our gridding and upscaling methods result in considerable improvements over uniform Cartesian models at the same coarsening level. This demonstrates that our gridding procedures correctly resolve the critical features in the reservoir and that our up-scaling techniques introduce appropriate effectivizations of subgrid heterogeneity. The tests also show that transmissibility upscaling generally produces better results than permeability upscaling, which is consistent with the previous findings for structured Cartesian grids and unstructured grids. Future work on this topic might be directed toward the development of more efficient 3-D grid generation techniques that allow a higher degree of local control on the grid structure.
He, Chuanping. (2004). Structured Flow-Based Gridding and Upscaling for Reservoir Simulation. Stanford Digital Repository. Available at: https://purl.stanford.edu/zy320vx8863
